title: Was Atlantis a real place?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine whether Atlantis was a real place. They trace Plato's 360 BC dialogues (Timaeus and Critias) that first describe Atlantis, the likelihood Plato drew on older stories or allegory, and the 1882 Ignatius Donnelly book that launched modern Atlantis speculation and placed Atlantis in many locations, including psychic Edgar Cayce's claims. They then argue Plato may have been inspired by Helike, a wealthy Greek city on the Gulf of Corinth that was destroyed by an earthquake and tsunami in 373 BC and later buried under silt from rivers, and that archaeologists have since uncovered it with several layered Roman, Byzantine, Bronze Age and Neolithic settlements. The episode also covers the Cornell-led search, the Spartan ships and Poseidon statue reports, and sea-level rise and submerged settlements such as Doggerland. A listener mail segment promotes the Celebrity Bookends fundraiser for the Cooperative for Education, and the episode closes with plugs for social media and the video podcast.
topics: ancient Greek city lost to earthquake

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to Atlantis
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck return from Texas and banter briefly, then introduce Atlantis, the Bahamas resort, and the question of whether the place was fictitious.

segments.title: Plato's account of Atlantis
segments.summary: Plato is the only ancient source for Atlantis, in his dialogue Timaeus, written around 360 BC. The hosts discuss his habit of mixing real places and events with literary license, and the story of Atlantis being sunk by Poseidon into the sea off the Pillars of Hercules.

segments.title: Ignatius Donnelly and the modern Atlantis craze
segments.summary: Ignatius Donnelly's 1882 book Atlantis: The Antediluvian World launched modern speculation, claiming Atlantis was the origin of civilization. Atlantis was later placed in many locations, and Edgar Cayce's psychic claims are described.

segments.title: Helike as a possible inspiration
segments.summary: The hosts suggest that a real event, the destruction of the Greek city Helike, may have inspired Plato's story, noting it was a powerful port on the Gulf of Corinth with a Poseidon cult and coinage.

segments.title: The destruction of Helike in 373 BC
segments.summary: Animals fled before an earthquake in December 373 BC, followed by a wave that submerged the city overnight. A rescue party found nothing but treetops, and ten Spartan ships in the port were gone. The city and its Poseidon statue remained visible underwater for centuries and were described by travelers and writers.

segments.title: Why Helike was vulnerable and got buried
segments.summary: The area's fresh water, fertile land and mild weather made it attractive, but two parallel fault lines made it prone to quakes. Silt from three rivers in the delta buried the city over the centuries, and the rising delta pushed the shoreline outward.

segments.title: Archaeological discovery and layered settlements
segments.summary: Archaeologists found several layered occupation levels above and below Helike, including Roman, Byzantine, Bronze Age and possibly Neolithic settlements. The search was led by Cornell professors in the late 1980s, with a Greek colleague correcting a translation that pointed to an inland lagoon instead of the gulf. Finds include a Roman road, coins, kilns, jugs and a sea wall, and excavation is ongoing.

segments.title: Wrap-up on Plato's inspiration and Man from Atlantis
segments.summary: Chuck argues Plato was likely inspired by Helike, given the event was well known and Plato lived in the region. The hosts mention the TV show Man from Atlantis and an HP Lovecraft story.

segments.title: Celebrity Bookends fundraiser
segments.summary: A listener describes a Facebook and Twitter campaign that sends a pair of bookends around the world to raise awareness and money for the Cooperative for Education in Guatemala.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact information
segments.summary: The hosts invite listeners to contact the show on Twitter, Facebook and email, and promote the video podcast Stuff from the Future.
